subtitle: Vie, amour et autorité déjà donnés au croyant

supporting_central_ideas.summary: Now that knowledge has increased, believers must learn better ways rather than continuing inherited but suboptimal customs.

Much church teaching focuses on preparing people to die well rather than teaching them to inherit resurrection life, citing selective use of 'flesh and blood cannot inherit' while omitting 'flesh and bone can inherit.'
Teaching that resurrection/inheritance is merely 'positional status' with no real experiential possibility is labeled antichrist heresy.
Jesus came not merely so believers live 'in the spirit' but so sons of men become sons of God, restoring what was lost when Adam fell.
The closing exhortation asserts that believers already possess eternal life — older, better, stronger and everlasting — that transcends physical death and bodily departure.
Preachers often illegitimately attach conditions (holiness, focus, preservation) onto God's declared unconditional love, though the text states no such condition.
Corruption (lying, conniving, deceit) comes naturally to fallen man without being taught, reflecting inherited fallen nature

supporting_topics.label: Physical resurrection and flesh/bone identity of Christ
God's unconditional love modeled on Jesus
Testimonies of resurrection from the dead

scope: Represents the proposed book better than the other three stored candidates: inherited/already-given life, love, and authority. Offices, practice, and closing testimonies are downstream of that thesis rather than a different book.
promise: Does not promise a topic absent from the SourceMap. It frames believers as already heirs of what the corpus teaches is already given.
ambiguity: French 'héritiers' can be read as legal inheritance, spiritual identity, or both. That is a working-title ambiguity, not an unsupported factual claim. Marketing quality is not judged here.
